doc.title: Ray Bryant interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, March 22, 1998

title: Joking with Marian McPartland about keys at Town Hall
summary: At the previous night's McPartland tribute he signalled four flats for 'Centerpiece'; jazz tunes are mostly in flat keys.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: I should explain to our listeners eventually, that I got to see you play last night with the Marian McPartland tribute which was a wonderful event. And when Sweets Edison came out, and I think you did a couple of numbers and then you were going to do “Centerpiece,” and Marian was at the other piano. And I saw you do this to her, you know? It was very deliberate that you were showing her something. Can you explain what that’s about?

Yeah, let me explain. Marian was actually joking, she said well “Centerpiece,” that’s one of the tunes that we played, that’s the tune that we played when Marian came out. It’s a Sweets’ original. Sweets Edison original. I played it with him many times before. Anybody knows it’s in the key of A flat. So Marian was just joking, she said, “What
key?” And so I said [gestures] which means four flats, key of A flat. So we were just joking back and forth and having some fun.
Right. I like that. What do you do for four sharps though?
Let’s see what key is four sharps? Four sharps, I don’t know.
It would be the key of — yeah right. Okay. For four sharps I’d go, no thank you.
That would be the key of E.
The key of E yeah. Unlikely to be playing in the key of E with a horn player.
You know we don’t delve too deeply into the sharp keys. Most jazz tunes are in flat keys.

I just think that’s so interesting to be on the stage at Town Hall, and the way jazz musicians work, you just go like this. Can you imagine Pavarotti coming out and going to his accompanist, you know.
